claims.text: Thermal aging of HfNbTaTiZr at 600–800 °C causes nanoscale clusters to form in situ.
The nanoscale clusters have a thermal expansion coefficient different from that of the surrounding matrix.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the clusters and matrix generates localized residual stresses during temperature cycling.
Cluster-induced localized stresses impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases the alloy's yield strength and hardening.
Cluster-induced residual stresses improve tensile creep resistance at approximately 1250 °C.
Cluster-induced residual stresses alter the alloy's overall elastic response.
The homogenized, solution-treated baseline is a single-phase homogeneous solid solution.
Aging above a threshold of approximately 600 °C is necessary for cluster nucleation.
Below the approximately 600 °C threshold, the alloy remains homogeneous and retains baseline properties.
Aged samples will contain nanoscale clusters detectable by microstructural analysis such as TEM.
Aged samples will have greater yield strength and hardening than solution-treated samples.
Aged samples will exhibit modified elastic moduli relative to solution-treated samples over the room-temperature-to-1100 K range.
Aged samples will exhibit altered thermal-expansion behavior relative to solution-treated samples.
Aged samples will exhibit improved tensile creep resistance at approximately 1250 °C relative to solution-treated samples.
Existing observations support nanoscale-cluster formation and its effects on the alloy's mechanical and thermoelastic properties.
